analysis.one_liner: Bars routine antibiotics in healthy livestock unless makers prove the practice cannot breed drug-resistant infections.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 53 cosponsors from both parties but never got a vote: it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from March 2002 until Congress adjourned in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Farmers routinely feed antibiotics like penicillin and tetracycline to healthy cattle, pigs, and poultry to speed growth and prevent disease in crowded conditions. Scientists, the National Academy of Sciences, and the American Medical Association have linked this practice to drug-resistant bacteria that can spread to people and make infections harder to treat. The bill would require drug makers to prove, within two years, that such routine use cannot harm human health, or lose federal approval — while leaving antibiotics for sick animals untouched. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who might ever need an antibiotic: the bill aims to keep existing drugs effective against infections by slowing the spread of resistant bacteria, and it would apply the same safety standard to farm drugs that already applies to human drugs. Consumers eating meat would also face fewer drug-resistant foodborne bacteria like salmonella and campylobacter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, and people who eat meat

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make federal approval of a farm antibiotic contingent on a 'reasonable certainty of no harm to human health' from antimicrobial resistance, a standard that did not previously apply to already-approved drugs.

It would rescind approval of routine, non-therapeutic uses of eight antibiotic classes — including penicillins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and bacitracin — within two years unless manufacturers prove safety, and it would end all fluoroquinolone use in poultry within 180 days unless proven safe.
The bill leaves treatment of sick animals intact: its definition of 'nontherapeutic use' covers only uses in the absence of disease, such as growth promotion and routine disease prevention.

The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Sciences conclusion that there is a link between antibiotics in food animals, bacterial resistance, and human disease, and note that the European Union had already banned growth-promotion uses of these drugs in 1999.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of the affected animal drugs would have to prove safety or abandon routine-use sales, and industrial livestock operations would lose growth promotion and routine disease prevention through feed, potentially raising production costs and meat prices. Bayer, the maker of a poultry fluoroquinolone, was already fighting the same withdrawal at the FDA.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal drug makers and industrial livestock farms

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a two-year deadline and, after an initial 180-day window, bars the FDA from considering newly submitted safety data for most drugs — a strict timeline that gives manufacturers little room to assemble the evidence the bill demands.

Phasing out growth promotion and routine disease prevention could raise production costs for livestock producers and, in turn, meat prices for consumers; the bill includes no transition assistance or study of those costs.

Banning routine disease prevention in crowded confinement operations could, critics argue, increase illness in herds and flocks unless farms also change how they raise animals — a shift the bill does not directly address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are asymmetric: losing antibiotic effectiveness is permanent and affects everyone, while the costs fall on a specific industry and likely show up as modest, one-time adjustments in meat production — the EU managed a comparable ban in 1999, which the bill's findings cite. The bill's hard deadlines and data cutoffs are unusually strict, but its core trade-off — proving a drug does not erode human medicine before using it routinely on healthy animals — mirrors the standard already applied to new drugs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee in March 2002; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on February 27, 2002, joined by Reps. Henry Waxman and Louise Slaughter as original sponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On March 13, 2002, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Health, where it remained; the only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in May 2002.

The bill attracted 53 cosponsors — 50 of 208 House Democrats and 3 of 223 House Republicans — but never received a subcommittee markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of feed antibiotics and industrial livestock operations kept the status quo: routine antibiotic use in healthy animals remains legal, and Bayer continued marketing its poultry fluoroquinolone while contesting the FDA's withdrawal effort.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal drug makers and large livestock operations

sides.party_line_note: Support was lopsidedly Democratic — 50 of 208 House Democrats cosponsored versus 3 of 223 Republicans — and the committee that declined to act was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would force makers of feed antibiotics to prove their routine-use products cannot breed human resistance within two years, or lose approval — directly threatening a product line sold by the pound to livestock operations. It leaves drugs for sick animals untouched but eliminates growth-promotion and routine-prevention sales that lack such proof.

Producers would lose growth promotion and routine disease prevention through feed, a low-cost input in confinement farming, and would have to adjust husbandry or accept slower growth and higher costs. Public-health evidence in the bill's findings suggests their current practice generates resistant bacteria that reach consumers.

Keeping existing antibiotics effective is a shared public good: the AMA, American Public Health Association, and other medical bodies had already opposed nontherapeutic farm antibiotic use, and the bill codifies their position into drug-approval law.
